opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most exciting shifts happening in robotics right now, and I like to frame it in terms of where the hard part of manipulation actually lives.

For a long time, the dominant paradigm was model-based: you write down the physics, you estimate the state of the world, object poses, contacts, friction, and then you plan or optimize a trajectory. That works beautifully in structured settings like a factory line, where you know exactly what the part is and where it is. But once you step into a kitchen or a home, the world becomes really hard to model. Deformable objects, articulated things like drawers, clutter, partial observability, contact-rich interactions. The modeling burden explodes, and every new task becomes a new engineering project.

What the data-driven shift says is: instead of hand-specifying all that structure, let's learn behaviors, and ideally the representations underneath them, from experience. Early on that meant reinforcement learning in simulation, and then increasingly imitation learning from human demonstrations, because RL in the real world is very expensive and specifying rewards for everyday tasks is surprisingly hard. In my own work, going back to my PhD days, a lot of the question was: how do you get robots to learn long-horizon tasks from demonstrations, and how do you make that data actually generalize rather than just memorize one trajectory?

What has really changed in the last few years is a combination of things. We got better policy architectures, things like diffusion policies and transformer-based models, that can capture the multimodality of human behavior. We got better and cheaper teleoperation and data collection tools. And there's this influence from vision and language, where we've seen that scale plus diverse data gives you surprising generalization. So the community started asking: can we get a similar effect in robotics?

But I'd say the honest picture is that robotics has a data problem that language and vision don't. There's no internet of robot actions. Every demonstration costs human time, robot time, and hardware. So a big part of my thinking, and my lab's work, is about where the data comes from and how to use it efficiently. Can we learn from human videos or from people just doing tasks with lightweight wearable devices, without a robot in the loop? Can we use simulation and generative models to multiply a small number of demos into many? Can we structure data so it's compositional, so that skills learned in one context transfer to another?

And I don't think it's purely data versus models. The interesting frontier is how to combine them, using structure where it genuinely helps, like geometry, task decomposition, or planning, and using learning where the world is too messy to hand-engineer. So to me the shift isn't just "throw more data at it." It's a change in where we put our effort: from engineering individual behaviors to engineering the data and learning systems that produce behaviors. That's a much more scalable bet, but it comes with real open questions about data, evaluation, and reliability that we're still working through.

r001.rationale: The response says learning can replace hand-specifying structure, but it ultimately advocates combining learning with useful structure and does not clearly state that explicit intermediate modeling can be dispensed with entirely.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it, the shift toward data-driven methods in manipulation is really a response to how badly the classical pipeline scaled. For a long time, the dominant approach was to decompose the problem: perceive the scene, estimate object poses, build a model of the world, plan a motion, then execute it with a controller. Each piece was engineered by hand, and each piece made assumptions. The moment those assumptions broke, say the object was deformable, or occluded, or just something you hadn't modeled, the whole stack fell apart. You could get beautiful results in a structured lab setup, but it never generalized to the messiness of a real kitchen or a real warehouse.

What data-driven methods changed is that instead of hand-specifying every component, you let the system learn the mapping from observations to actions directly from experience. That experience can come from human demonstrations, from simulation, from the robot trying things itself, or increasingly from large passive datasets like video. The appeal is that the model can absorb the long tail of situations that you could never anticipate as an engineer. We saw this happen in vision and language first, and manipulation is following, just more slowly because collecting robot data is expensive and physically grounded.

I'd add two caveats, though. First, the "shift" isn't really a replacement of structure with data. The most successful systems I've seen combine the two. You still care about things like object-centric representations, task decomposition, or action abstractions, but you learn them rather than hard-code them, or you use them as inductive biases that make learning sample-efficient. Second, data for robotics isn't just "more is better." The question of what data to collect, how diverse it is, and how it's labeled or structured ends up mattering as much as the model architecture. A lot of my own work has been about that gap: how do you get useful demonstration data, how do you learn skills that can be composed, and how do you make the learned policy robust when the world doesn't look like the training set.

So, in short, I see the shift as moving the burden from the human engineer's priors to the data, and then the interesting research question becomes which priors you still want to keep and where you get the data to fill in the rest.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning mappings from observations to actions, but says successful systems still use structure such as object representations, task decomposition, or action abstractions. It does not clearly state that explicit intermediate modeling can be dispensed with entirely.

astra-6.text:
I think the shift is really about where the knowledge for manipulating objects comes from. Traditionally, we tried to put that knowledge into the system ourselves: model the object, model the contact, and design a controller. That works well when the environment is structured. But once you’re dealing with everyday objects, there are so many variations that it becomes difficult to anticipate all of them.

With data-driven methods, we’re asking whether robots can learn some of that knowledge from examples and experience. Instead of specifying exactly how to grasp every object, we can learn a policy that connects what the robot sees to what it should do.

But that also changes the bottleneck. Now we have to ask: Where does the data come from? How diverse is it? And does learning from that data actually help the robot handle a situation it hasn’t seen before? Collecting physical interaction data is much harder than collecting text or images, because the robot has to act in the world, and those actions take time and can fail.

So I see it as a shift in how we build capability, rather than a reason to discard everything we know about robotics. The interesting opportunity is combining learning with the structure we already understand about geometry, physics, and control.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning policies from examples, but it does not say data-driven manipulation may dispense entirely with explicit intermediate modeling. It instead suggests combining learning with existing structure in geometry, physics, and control.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the shift is really from trying to specify every detail of a robot’s behavior to building systems that can learn those details from experience. In manipulation, that matters because the world is incredibly varied. An object might have a different shape, the friction might change, or something might move when you touch it. It’s very difficult to write rules that cover all of those situations.

With data-driven methods, we can learn from demonstrations and interaction, and potentially reuse that experience across different tasks. But that also changes the bottleneck: How do we collect useful data? How do we cover the situations the robot will encounter? And how do we know that a learned policy will work outside its training conditions?

So I wouldn’t frame it as abandoning everything we know about robotics. The interesting direction is combining learning with structure—with geometry, physics, planning, and control—so that robots can benefit from data while still behaving reliably.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning behavior from data but does not say this may eliminate explicit intermediate modeling entirely. It instead advocates combining learning with geometry, physics, planning, and control.
